title: Omega Boost
subtitle: Polyphony leaves the road for open space
summary: Omega Boost is Polyphony Digital's PlayStation shooting game, first released in Japan on 22 April 1999. The player controls a flying mecha through waves of enemies, using movement and target selection to survive a rapid sequence of combat situations. Mechanical designs by Shōji Kawamori give the central machine a recognisable character. It is an unusual work from a studio associated with Gran Turismo, turning its attention from racing cars to a science-fiction action spectacle. The immediate task is to understand the surrounding formation quickly enough to remove its threats before they close in.
body: Omega Boost is Polyphony Digital's PlayStation shooting game, first released in Japan on 22 April 1999. The player controls a flying mecha through waves of enemies, using movement and target selection to survive a rapid sequence of combat situations. Mechanical designs by Shōji Kawamori give the central machine a recognisable character. It is an unusual work from a studio associated with Gran Turismo, turning its attention from racing cars to a science-fiction action spectacle. The immediate task is to understand the surrounding formation quickly enough to remove its threats before they close in.

Enemy groups arrive in a fixed sequence, allowing the player to learn their patterns, but the order of targets within each wave remains a choice. Movement offers room to adjust position and bring another opponent into the attack. Some stages allow greater freedom while others constrain speed or direction, changing the conditions without abandoning the central control of the machine. Repeated attempts reveal how a formation is assembled. The player can then act earlier, turning a first impression of visual chaos into a more deliberate sequence of targets and evasive movements.

Yasushi Taki and Zaika Tei directed the project, with Kazunori Yamauchi producing and Jun Kitagawa composing the music. The main campaign contains nine stages and additional unlockable special missions. Some reviewers found that scope too brief or the action too simple, while the presentation showed another use for the studio's technical experience. International releases arrived in September 1999. Omega Boost remains Polyphony's singular departure from racing, making it a useful glimpse of how the team approached speed and motion when the vehicle could move through three-dimensional space instead of following a road.

A short detour with a distinct machine
